title: Looking for Learning Needs Judgement
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Martin Skelton uses a Wendell Berry poem to make a point about how teachers and school leaders judge whether learning is happening. He recaps the three-part shape of his Looking for Learning series, then argues that evidence is non-negotiable for any learning-focused school but that much of it requires professional judgement rather than hard numbers. Judgements are evaluations, not facts, and they improve when several perspectives are combined, which is why moderation and conversation with the teacher and students matter. His main warning is about sticky prejudices, the ready-made thoughts about particular children, classes and colleagues that make us see what we expect. The remedy is a beginner's mind that looks afresh, slowly and with a small number of students, because learning, like fishing, rewards patience.
points: Evidence about learning is essential, but much of it depends on thoughtful professional judgement and not just hard numbers.
Judgements are stronger when several people compare them, which is the role of moderation and shared conversation.
Prior beliefs about students and colleagues become sticky and can blind observers to what is actually happening in a lesson.
Watching a few students carefully for longer gives more reliable evidence of learning than rushing past every desk.
quotes: Much of the evidence around learning requires judgement, a thoughtful consideration of what we are seeing and what it might be telling us. People are often suspicious of judgement; they want hard numbers.
Evidence is a non-negotiable if we are genuinely learning-focused. But learning-related evidence is not without its flaws.

First, judgements aren’t ‘right’ in the sense that ‘Paris is the capital of France’ is right. Judgements are evaluations of different kinds of evidence which lead to a reasonable conclusion even if we can’t say it is right.
It’s not always a good idea to act on the judgement of just one person; a better judgement usually arrives after a number of different perspectives have been taken into account.
These ready-made, already sticky, thoughts about children and students can cause us to rush to judgement and sometimes ignore what we are seeing in front of us.
We have to develop what Buddhists and others have described as a Beginners’ Mind, the ability to do whatever we can to see things unfiltered by our own sticky prejudices and previous learning.

A little like fishing, we have to be patient, waiting and watching to see if any learning is going to bite. We get a more reliable evidence base about learning by looking at a smaller number of students openly and carefully than we do trying to make rushed judgements about everyone.
If only we can allow ourselves to see it, yesterday’s student who didn’t seem to be learning anything may be the student who is making a breakthrough today.
